title: Heat acclimation decay and re-induction: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Daanen HAM, Racinais S, Periard JD
population: 12 studies of heat acclimation (at least 5 days) followed by decay (at least 7 days) and, in 8 studies, re-acclimation; outcomes heart rate, core temperature, sweat rate
findings: End-exercise HR adaptations decreased 2.3% per day of decay and core temperature adaptations 2.6% per day (adaptation scored 0% = acclimated, 100% = unacclimated).
About 2.5% of HR and core temperature adaptations are lost per decay day (earlier literature: 1 day lost per 2 days of decay).
Decay in sweat rate was not related to the number of decay days.

Five or more acclimation days are sufficient to cause adaptations in HR and core temperature; longer daily exposure duration (and lower exposure intensity) made core temperature adaptations more sustainable.
Re-acclimation was 8-12 times faster than decay for HR and core temperature; it may provide a practical, less disruptive way to maintain acclimation before competition (e.g. in a taper).
limitations: Only 12 studies (8 on re-acclimation); no protocol standardization; regression on heterogeneous designs; healthy trained adults.
implications: Decay model: credit of HR/core-temperature acclimation falls by about 2.5% of the acclimated state per day after the last heat session (2.3% HR, 2.6% core temperature). Setting credit to zero at about 40 days is a design extrapolation (100/2.5) beyond the data, flagged as such.
Schedule heat exposure close to the goal race; a short top-up block is far quicker than the original and fits a taper.
The 5-day minimum is a lower bound; the plan default remains the 7-14 day block.

verification.notes: Crossref (online 2017-11, print 2018-02) and Europe PMC abstract re-fetched. Added the intensity and taper statements from the abstract; the 40-day cutoff is the researcher's extrapolation and is labelled as such.
